entries.name: mcp__claude_ai_Linear__save_issue
entries.description: Create or update a Linear issue. If `id` is provided, updates the existing issue; otherwise creates a new one. When creating, `team` is required, and `title` is required unless `template` is set. Note: use `assignee` (not `assigneeId`) to set the assignee — it accepts a user ID, name, email, or "me".

id.description: Only for updating an existing issue. Pass the issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). Do NOT pass this parameter when creating a new issue.

title.description: Issue title (required when creating, unless template is set)

description.description: Content as Markdown. Do not escape the string — use literal newlines and special characters, not escape sequences. To mention a user, use @displayName (e.g., @johndoe)

patch.description: Partial edits applied to the current content, in order and atomically (one failing operation aborts the whole save). Every anchor string must match the current content exactly once. Only valid on update, in place of the full content/description field

old_string.description: Exact text to replace. Must match the current content exactly once

new_string.description: Replacement text. Empty string deletes the match

replace_all.description: Replace every occurrence instead of requiring a unique match

anchor.description: Exact text to insert before. Must match the current content exactly once

text.description: Text to insert directly before the anchor. Include separators (e.g. "\n\n")

anchor.description: Exact text to insert after. Must match the current content exactly once

text.description: Text to insert directly after the anchor. Include separators (e.g. "\n\n")
Text to insert at the very start of the content
Text to insert at the very end of the content

from.description: Exact text where the range starts (inclusive). Must match exactly once

to.description: Exact text where the range ends (exclusive, stays in place). Must match exactly once after `from`

new_string.description: Text replacing the range. Empty string deletes it

team.description: Team name or ID (required when creating)

template.description: Template name or ID. Applied on create only. The template fills in the content, fields, and sub-issues server-side. A `description` replaces the template body rather than merging with it, but an empty `description` keeps the template body. Labels merge with the template's own

cycle.description: Cycle name, number, or ID. Null to remove

project.description: Project name, ID, identifier (e.g., P-ENG-123), or slug. Null to remove

assignee.description: User ID, name, email, or "me". Null to remove

delegate.description: Agent name or ID. When the user asks to delegate to "Linear" or "the Linear agent", this refers to the "Linear" app user specifically. Null to remove

labels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]). Replaces the full label set; existing labels not included are removed. Omit to leave labels unchanged. Cannot be combined with addLabels/removeLabels; prefer those for incremental changes

addLabels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]) to add. Append-only; existing labels are never removed. Cannot be combined with a team change

removeLabels.description: Label names or IDs as a JSON array of strings (e.g. ["Bug", "Urgent"]) to remove. Only valid when updating an existing issue. Cannot be combined with a team change

dueDate.description: Due date (ISO format). On update, pass null to remove the due date

slaBreachesAt.description: ISO-8601 timestamp when the SLA will breach. On update, pass null to remove the SLA

slaType.description: SLA day counting type: "all" or "onlyBusinessDays". Only use with slaBreachesAt; null means unset

parentId.description: Parent issue ID or identifier (e.g., LIN-123). Null to remove

estimate.description: Issue estimate value. On create, pass null or omit for no estimate. On update, pass null to clear the estimate; omitting leaves it unchanged. 0 is a real estimate only on teams that allow zero estimates.

links.description: Link attachments to add [{url, title}]. Append-only; existing links are never removed

setReleases.description: Replace all releases on the issue with these. Cannot be combined with addReleases/removeReleases

addReleases.description: Release IDs or slugs to add. Append-only; existing releases are never removed

removeReleases.description: Release IDs or slugs to remove. Only valid when updating an existing issue

blocks.description: Issue IDs/identifiers this blocks. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

blockedBy.description: Issue IDs/identifiers blocking this. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

relatedTo.description: Related issue IDs/identifiers. Append-only; existing relations are never removed

duplicateOf.description: Duplicate of issue ID/identifier. Null to remove

removeBlockedBy.description: Issue IDs/identifiers to remove as blockers of this issue

{"id":"SMA-837","uuid":"ed843ebc-e7b9-4193-a8d4-4fb93b4a4533","title":"Bedrock builder: add a family override for opaque model IDs such as application inference profile ARNs","description":"The Bedrock provider detects the model family from the model ID string. After <issue id="6d61b0db-1e68-42ac-8e2a-ed93fe10f8fc" label="SMA-832" href="https://linear.app/smaschek/issue/SMA-832/bedrock-detects-global-inference-profile-ids-as-modelfamilyunknown" />, this works for every geographic prefix and for foundation-model, inference-profile and prompt-router ARNs.

Some model IDs are opaque. Examples are application inference profile ARNs (`arn:aws:bedrock:<region>:<acct>:application-inference-profile/<id>`), provisioned-throughput ARNs and custom-model ARNs. For these IDs, the family is always `ModelFamily::Unknown`.

## Effect

* Structured-output synthesis and forced tool choice are off. `build_request` reads the detected family (`translate/mod.rs`), not the capabilities.
* `BedrockModelBuilder::capabilities(...)` changes only what `capabilities()` reports. It does not turn on the family-gated request behavior. So a user of an opaque ID has no way to turn on these features.

## Required behavior

* Add a builder method, for example `BedrockModelBuilder::family(ModelFamily)`. When it is set, the builder uses that family and does not detect one from the ID.
* The override controls the request translation and the default capabilities, in the same way as a detected family.
* Document the method in the crate README and in the mdBook Bedrock section.

## Acceptance criteria

* A unit test shows that an application inference profile ARN with `.family(ModelFamily::Anthropic)` gets structured-output synthesis and a forced `toolChoice`.
* Without the override, the result is unchanged.

# Brainstorming

You are very good at building. You build what you believe your human
partner wants, and that belief is usually thinner than it feels. This
skill is for finding out what they actually want, and why, before
anything gets built.

People often haven't finished working out what they want. Good questions
help them think it through. When you understand the why, you make the
hundred decisions they never mention the way they would have made them.

## First: What Do You Actually Know?

Before you reply, ask yourself: what do I know about what they want, and
why?

- **Everything that matters is in the request** ("make the icon cornflower
  blue"). This is a quick, clear task. Do it, and say what you did.
- **Something non-trivial is missing.** Start the conversation.

Before you start implementing, you must, in order:

1. Lay out the approaches in a message of their own, and have your
   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

   human partner pick one (see Lay out the approaches).
2. Write the design doc, short or full (see Size the Work).
3. Get their approval of that doc.
4. Invoke the superpowers:writing-plans skill.

If nothing is open when you write your first message and there's one
sensible way, steps 1 to 3 happen in that message (see Your First
Message).

Two things aren't implementing: a spike they said yes to (see Spike to
feel things out), and doing what they asked once they've opted out of
the questions.

## Look Before You Ask

In an existing project, or when they've given you context (a spec, a plan,
a handoff, files they pointed at, earlier conversation), dig in before your
first message. Read what they referred to and the code or material it
connects to, and keep reading until you can explain how the relevant
parts work today and what this change would touch. Never ask what the
project or their context already answers, or reopen what they've
already decided.

## Your First Message

Move the work forward, with one of these:

- **They've already said what they want** (a spec, a plan, a detailed
  request): aim for about 200 words for the whole message. Echo their
  request back in your own words, so they can see whether you've got its
  shape: what they want, who it's for, and why, as far as they've said.
  Add what you found that bears on it: how the relevant parts work today
  and what the change would touch. If you found something they may not
  have considered that would change what they're asking for or how it
  has to be built, like a constraint, a conflict, or a cheaper path, say
  so plainly. How to build it comes later, once you understand what they
  want (see Lay out the approaches). End with one line inviting
  corrections. Then, if they haven't told you why they want it, even if
  you can guess, ask about that: one open question in their own terms,
  with nothing to pick from. If they have told you, and their request
  and the project leave open something whose answer would change what
  gets built, ask about the one that would change it most; when its
  choices can be named, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
  and which you'd pick. If nothing like that is open, there's one
  sensible way: end with the short design itself (the approach, a line on
  why the others don't fit, and the design in a few lines) and ask them
  to approve it. Their approval covers the approach and the design: write
  the short design doc as approved and go on to the plan.
  Specs are often incomplete, so confirm before you build on one.
- **They haven't:** one open question, in their own terms, about the
  biggest thing their request leaves unsettled. Say why you're asking:
  what the answer would change about what you build. For "a website for
  my bakery": "If it's mostly for people deciding whether to stop by,
  I'd lead with hours and what's in the case today; taking orders is a
  different site. What do you want someone to do when they land on it?"

How the message ends depends on whether their message asked for
brainstorming:

- **They asked for it** (by name, by invoking it, or by asking for a
  design discussion): end there. They want this conversation.
- **They didn't:** they may not want a conversation at all. End with a
  light, one-line offer to just get going instead, like
  "Or if you'd rather I just dive in, say so." If they take you up on
  it, this skill is done: state any significant how-it-gets-made choice
  (platform, language, medium) in one plain line, then do what they
  asked through the normal workflow.

That's the whole message.

## The Conversation

Ask a question only when the answer would change what gets built and
neither the request nor the project answers it. Otherwise, state your
call and your reason as a proposal they can correct, and move the work
forward. Process steps are always your calls: writing things up, where
files go, looking further, how to show something. Do them and say so.
Ask one at a time. Use plain language, pitched just a little above where
your human partner is. Match their vocabulary; never use process jargon.
You never need to quote this skill to your human partner.

Be clear and concise. Lead with what matters. Avoid jargon. When you
report what you found, give them the most important findings and offer
the rest.

**Get them describing.** Until you know why they want it, ask open
questions, with no example answers attached. Their own words carry
intent that your options can't. Once you know why, when a decision has
choices you can name, sketch each concretely, with what it trades off
and which you'd pick. When they say "just guess" or "what do you think?",
propose something concrete.

**How it gets made.** Every project rests on choices about medium, tools,
materials, and resources: the platform, programming language, and
libraries for an app; the medium for a piece of art. Read from how they
talk which of those choices they want to make. Someone who raises the how
or asks about trade-offs wants the options with your pick. Someone who
talks about outcomes is handing you the how: make those calls and state
each in a line. When there's existing work, build on what it already
uses. Any choice you make goes in the design as your call, never as
something they agreed to.

**Ground to cover.** This is territory, not a script. Never read these
out as questions:

- what kind of thing this is, and what makes it special
- why now, and what success looks like to them
- goals, non-goals, and anti-goals (what would make this a failure even
  if it technically works)
- prior art: what they've seen elsewhere, loved or hated
- current state: what exists now, what they've tried
- the details they care about

**Make every question specific** to their project and what they've told
you. Ask Socratically, the way a sharp colleague would: build each
question on their last answer or on something you found, so it helps
them think through a consequence or a case they may have missed
("Voting closes before the meeting, and two members joined this month.
Does someone who joins mid-round get a vote?"). When the reason isn't
already plain, say what you're hoping to learn or what the answer would
change. A proposal they can correct, plus your reason for it, often
beats a question.

**Do recon.** Once you have a bit of grounding and looking further
would help, go look: deeper into their codebase or project, their own
files and data, or the web. Say what you looked for and what you found.

**Lay out the approaches.** Once you understand what they want, and
before you write anything up, put the ways of building it in a message
of its own. Come up with several real alternatives and drop the weak
ones, including any that work against why they want it and any the
existing work rules out. Sketch the two or three that remain concretely
enough to picture, grounded in what the project actually does, with what
each trades off. Recommend one and say why, then ask which way they want
to go; if they've handed you the how, say you'll go with your pick
instead. When there's genuinely one sensible way, say so in that
message and explain why the others don't fit; the design comes in the
next one. This is for how it gets built; for what they want, get them
describing first.

**Show, don't tell.** Whenever seeing would help more than reading,
sketch it in text: a few lines of what they'd see. Offer the visual
companion (below) when the look itself is theirs to decide:

- something they'll look at: a screen, a page, a printout, a sign
- a layout or arrangement: of a screen, a room, a schedule
- a flow or a sequence of steps
- options that would look different from each other
- a structure that's easier to see than read: a diagram, a timeline, a map

Once they've accepted, use it for mockups to react to, side-by-side
options, and throwaway prototypes they can click.

**Spike to feel things out.** Agentic work is waterfall, but very, very
fast. A quick throwaway build is often the cheapest way to learn what
they want or whether something works. Offer one when it would help.
When they just want to spike, get out of the way. Spikes get no tests
or minimal ones, aren't bulletproof, and skip the plan, implementation,
and review process. Bring what the spike taught you back into the
conversation.

## Play It Back

Play back as you go. As soon as you understand one part well enough to
describe it (what it's for and who it serves, say, or how one piece
behaves), describe that part back in about 200-300 words, then return to
questions about the next part. Playback and questions alternate through
the whole conversation; the last chunk covers whatever is left.

Only what they said goes in as theirs. Anything you filled in goes in
as your proposal, with your reason. End each chunk by asking what's wrong
or missing.

Before you send a chunk, check it: does it describe something they'll
look at, like a page, a screen, a schedule, or a printout? If so, put a
text sketch next to the description. If the look itself is theirs to
decide and they haven't seen the visual companion offer yet, send the
offer instead (its own message, below) and hold the chunk for the next
message. Once they've accepted, put a mockup next to the description.

## Size the Work

Once you understand what they want and they've picked an approach, say
how big the work is in plain words. They can override it.

| Size | The design doc |
|------|----------------|
| A small change | a short one: what you already covered together, written down |
| A project | the full written design (below) |

Short or full, the design doc has an **Approaches** part: the two or
three ways you considered building it, what each trades off, which one
they picked, and why. They pick in the conversation, before you write
the doc.

If it grows mid-task, stop, say so, and step up a size.

If this is really several independent projects, say so, agree on an
order, and brainstorm them one at a time.

## The Written Design

Write a plain document a talented builder in the domain could plan
from without going back to your human partner. Cover:

- intent and the why
- goals, non-goals, anti-goals
- constraints
- approaches (above)
- the parts of the how they decided, as they decided them
- what's left to the builder

For a small change, the short design covers the same points in a line
or two each and goes straight to your human partner, without the
builder check.

**Where it goes:** in a software repo,
`docs/superpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`, committed.
Otherwise, pick a sensible place and say where. Your human partner's
preferences override both.

**Builder check** (for a project): dispatch a fresh subagent with
`builder-check-prompt.md` in this directory. When you tell your human
partner you're writing it up, say a reviewer will read it first and you
may come back once with a few questions. Don't hand over the document
until the check is back. Sort what the builder asks into three piles:

- **Answered already** by the conversation or the project: put the answer
  in the document.
- **Minor:** a sensible builder could settle it without changing what gets
  built. Settle it yourself and mark it in the document as your call.
- **Theirs:** only your human partner can answer it, and the answer changes
  what gets built.

Bring the "theirs" pile in one message, most important first. Update the
document with their answers, then hand it over with a short list of the
calls you made so they can check those while reading. That's the only
round of questions the check produces. Without a subagent tool, read the
document as that builder yourself.

<HARD-GATE>
Nothing gets built until your human partner approves the design doc:
the short one for a small change, the full one for a project.
Building includes writing product code, scaffolding, installing
dependencies, creating projects, and invoking an implementation skill.
Reading and exploring are fine.

Two exceptions. If they opted out of the questions, the skill is done
and the gate goes with it. A spike they said yes to may be built; it
stays labeled throwaway, and keeping what it produced is a new request
that comes back through this gate.

After the design doc is approved, the next step is the plan: invoke
superpowers:writing-plans and no other skill.
</HARD-GATE>

## Red Flags

| Thought | Reality |
|---------|---------|
| "I'll offer a menu of what they might want" | Options steer. Ask them to describe it first. |
| "I'll fill in sensible defaults" | Good. Say them out loud. A default they never heard is one they couldn't reject. |
| "I've answered their questions, so I'll write the doc" | Lay out the approaches first, in a message of their own (or, when nothing was open from the start, in your first message's short design). |
| "I should explain the process first" | Ask your question. The process shows itself. |
| "They said 'sounds good' to the idea" | Approval covers what you showed them. A design doc you haven't written isn't approved. |
| "The spike works, I'll keep building on it" | Keeping it is a new request. Back through the gate. |

## Visual Companion

A browser tab for showing mockups, diagrams, and prototypes. It's a
tool, not a mode: accepting it doesn't send every question to the
browser.

**Offer it just-in-time.** Offer it the first time one of the moments
above comes up, never upfront. The offer is its own message with nothing
else in it:

> "This might be easier if I show you. Want me to open a browser tab with some mockups?"

If they decline, stay in text and don't offer again unless they raise it.

**Per question, ask: would they understand this better by seeing it?**
Mockups, layouts, diagrams, and side-by-side designs go in the browser.
Requirements, scope, tradeoffs, and conceptual choices stay in text. A
question about a UI topic isn't automatically a visual question.

If they accept, read `visual-companion.md` in this directory before
starting the server.

## Model families

The crate detects the model family from the Bedrock model ID and routes capability flags accordingly:

| Family | Examples | Structured output | Forced tool choice |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Anthropic` | `anthropic.claude-*`, `us.anthropic.*`, `global.anthropic.*` | yes (forced-tool synthesis; native output on Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5) | yes, except Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 |
| `AmazonNova` | `amazon.nova-*` | yes (forced-tool synthesis) | yes |
| `Mistral` | `mistral.mistral-*` | yes (forced-tool synthesis) | yes |
| `AmazonTitan` | `amazon.titan-*` | no (degrades to text) | no |
| `Llama` | `meta.llama*` | no (degrades to text) | no |
| `Cohere` | `cohere.command-*` | no (degrades to text) | no |
| `Unknown` | anything unrecognized | no | no |

Detection reads the first segment of the model ID. If the first segment is not a provider name, detection reads the second segment. This skips a geographic prefix. The known prefixes are `us.`, `eu.`, `apac.`, `jp.`, `au.`, `ca.`, `in.` and `global.`. A future prefix works too. For an ARN, detection uses the resource ID, which is the text after the last `/`. An opaque ARN, such as an application inference profile ARN, gives `Unknown`.

## Structured output and the schema rewriter

For families that support forced-tool-choice (`Anthropic`, `AmazonNova`, `Mistral`), structured output (`ResponseFormat::JsonSchema`) is synthesized as a hidden tool call — the model is forced to call a reserved internal tool whose input schema is the user-supplied JSON Schema. Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5 reject a forced tool choice. These models use native output instead (see the next section).

For tool input schemas, Bedrock's Converse validator rejects JSON Schemas that use `$ref`/`$defs`, `oneOf`/`anyOf`/`allOf`, or certain other keywords (such as `$schema`, `format`, `examples`). The `rewrite_tool_schema` function (exposed publicly for testing and advanced use) rewrites schemas inline: inlining `$ref` references, collapsing combinators into a flat object, and stripping unsupported keywords — so schemars-generated schemas for tagged enums and generic structs pass validation.

### Native structured output (Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5)

These models reject a forced `toolChoice`. For these models, the crate puts the `JsonSchema` in `outputConfig.textFormat`. The native output schema accepts `$ref`/`$defs` and `anyOf`.

On a finalizing turn, the crate can add a hidden anchor tool with no `toolChoice`. If the model calls this anchor, the provider logs a warning. `outputConfig` does not constrain the text of that call.

An Anthropic model ID that is not on the list can also reject the forced choice. This costs one rejected request for each `BedrockModel` handle. After that, the handle and its clones use native output. The crate logs one warning. Only a `ValidationException` with one of the two known rejection texts changes the handle. The request must also send a forced choice. Other errors go to the caller and do not change the handle. A request that fails locally does not reach Bedrock, so it cannot change the handle. For example, `JsonSchema` together with `ToolChoice::Tool` fails locally on a forced-choice handle.

The crate rewrites the schema before it sends the schema:

- It adds `additionalProperties: false` to object nodes. It does not add the keyword to a node that has `patternProperties` or `propertyNames`, to a node in an `allOf` composition or to any node below an `allOf` member, to a `const` or `enum` node or any node below it, or to a node whose `required` names a property that `properties` does not declare. It also does not add the keyword to an object node next to `oneOf` or `anyOf`. The branches of such a node stay open too. Limit: a `$defs` entry outside an `allOf` member is still closed, also when a `$ref` in the member points to it. That closed entry can reject a property that another member declares. Do not use a `$ref` to an object in an `allOf` member if the other members add properties.
- It changes `oneOf` to `anyOf`.
- It removes `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf`, `maxItems`, `uniqueItems`, `minItems` above 1, and `not`, `if`, `then` and `else`.

An open object in an `allOf` composition can cause a `ValidationException` from Bedrock. You cannot close each member, because each closed member would reject the properties of the other members. Put the properties into one closed object instead.

The server does not enforce the removed limits. The agent loop does not evaluate the JSON schema. It checks that the result deserializes into the output type, and asks for a repair when it does not. A removed limit that only the schema states (for example a `schemars` range attribute) is not checked. Add your own validation for such a limit. The change from `oneOf` to `anyOf` also accepts a value that matches more than one branch. If your code needs exactly one branch to match, validate the result against the original schema.

Bedrock rejects these shapes with its own error: maps (`HashMap`, or `additionalProperties` that is `true` or a schema), `patternProperties`, `propertyNames`, tuples (`prefixItems`), the schemas `true` and `{}`, and recursive types. The crate does not rewrite them.

On this path, `JsonObject` degrades to text. User tools stay callable when `JsonSchema` is set. The crate omits `ToolChoice::Required` and `ToolChoice::Tool` with a warning. `ToolChoice::Tool` with a name that is not a defined tool is still an error. `ToolChoice::Required` with no tools and no response format is still an error. With a structured response format, the crate omits it with a warning.

When a model's family does not support forced-tool-choice, a `JsonSchema` response format degrades silently to a text response; no error is returned.

Reasoning content surfaced by the model (e.g. Claude extended-thinking responses) is delivered as `ModelEvent::ReasoningDelta` in the stream — no extra configuration is required on this provider.

After that, the handle and its clones use native output. The crate logs one warning. Only a `ValidationException` with one of the two known rejection texts changes the handle. The request must also send a forced choice. Other errors go to the caller and do not change the handle. A request that fails locally does not reach Bedrock, so it cannot change the handle. For example, `JsonSchema` together with `ToolChoice::Tool` fails locally on a forced-choice handle.

The crate rewrites the schema before it sends the schema:

- It adds `additionalProperties: false` to object nodes. It does not add the keyword to a node that has `patternProperties` or `propertyNames`, to a node in an `allOf` composition or to any node below an `allOf` member, to a `const` or `enum` node or any node below it, or to a node whose `required` names a property that `properties` does not declare. - It changes `oneOf` to `anyOf`.
- It removes `minimum`, `maximum`, `exclusiveMinimum`, `exclusiveMaximum`, `multipleOf`, `maxItems`, `uniqueItems`, `minItems` above 1, and `not`, `if`, `then` and `else`.

An open object in an `allOf` composition can cause a `ValidationException` from Bedrock. You cannot close each member, because each closed member would reject the properties of the other members. Put the properties into one closed object instead.

The server does not enforce the removed limits. The agent loop does not evaluate the JSON schema. It checks that the result deserializes into the output type, and asks for a repair when it does not. # SMA-837: Bedrock builder family override for opaque model IDs

Status: draft. Size: a small change (one crate, one new builder method, docs).

## Intent

The Bedrock provider detects the model family from the model ID string. Some
model IDs are opaque: application inference profile ARNs
(`arn:aws:bedrock:<region>:<acct>:application-inference-profile/<id>`),
provisioned-throughput ARNs and custom-model ARNs. For these IDs the detected
family is always `ModelFamily::Unknown`.

`build_request` reads the family, not the capabilities. So for an opaque ID,
structured-output synthesis and forced tool choice are off.
`BedrockModelBuilder::capabilities(...)` changes only what `capabilities()`
reports. A user of an opaque ID has no way to turn on these features. This
change gives that user a way.

## Goals

- Add `BedrockModelBuilder::family(ModelFamily) -> Self`. When it is set, the
  builder uses that family and does not detect one from the model ID.
- The override has the same effect as a detected family on all three family
  consumers:
  1. `Config.family`, which the request translation reads (`translate/mod.rs`):
     schema ruleset, structured-output synthesis, forced `toolChoice`.
  2. The default capabilities (`caps_for(family)`).
  3. `ForcedChoicePolicy.family`, which the SMA-839 rule-B fallback reads
     (`fallback.rs` checks `policy.family() == ModelFamily::Anthropic`).
- Without the override, the behavior is unchanged.
- Document the method in the rustdoc, the crate README ("Model families") and
  the mdBook Bedrock section (`docs/book/src/concepts/model-providers.md`,
  "Family-gated structured output").

## Non-goals

- No new detection rules for opaque IDs. An opaque ID contains no family.
- No change to `ModelFamily` (it is already public and `#[non_exhaustive]`;
  callers can name its variants).
- No AWS call to resolve an application inference profile to its model. The
  builder stays synchronous and offline.
- No hand version bump. release-plz gives the additive change a patch bump.

## Anti-goals

- The override must not split the family: the request translation, the
  capabilities and the policy must never see different families.
- `.capabilities(...)` must keep its current meaning and precedence.

## Design

1. `BedrockModelBuilder` gets a field `family_override: Option<ModelFamily>`,
   default `None`.
2. `family(mut self, f: ModelFamily) -> Self` sets it. A second call replaces
   the first value, the same as the other builder setters.
3. In `build()`, step 3 becomes:
   `let family = self.family_override.unwrap_or_else(|| ModelFamily::from_model_id(&self.model_id));`
   The existing "model family not detected" debug log fires only when no
   override is set and detection gives `Unknown`. When an override is set, log
   one `debug!` that names the override family and the model ID.
4. `caps_for(family)` and `ForcedChoicePolicy::new(&model_id, family)` receive
   the effective family. So they agree with `Config.family`.
5. Capability precedence: `.capabilities(...)` > `caps_for(override family)` >
   `caps_for(detected family)`.
6. `.family(ModelFamily::Unknown)` is valid. It turns the family-gated
   behavior off for an ID that detection would classify.

### Static rule A with an override (my call)

`rejects_forced_tool_choice(model_id)` reads only the model ID, and it is
`true` only when the detected family is `Anthropic` and the ID names Claude
Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5. Two consequences:

- Opaque ID plus `.family(Anthropic)`: rule A is off, because the ID does not
  name the model. The first structured-output request sends a forced
  `toolChoice`. If the profile points at Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5, Bedrock
  rejects it once, and rule B moves the handle to native output (this works
  because the policy carries the override family). The cost is one rejected
  request per handle. Document this.
- Non-opaque Sonnet 5.5 ID plus a non-Anthropic override (a user error): rule
  A would select the native path for a non-Anthropic family. To keep the
  family consistent, `ForcedChoicePolicy::new` sets the static rule only when
  the effective family is `Anthropic`:
  `rejects_static = family == ModelFamily::Anthropic && rejects_forced_tool_choice(model_id)`.
  Without an override this is the same value as today, because
  `rejects_forced_tool_choice` is already `false` for a non-Anthropic detected
  family.

## Approaches considered

- **A. Builder method `family(ModelFamily)` that feeds all consumers (chosen).**
  The ticket names this design. It is one field and one resolved value.
- **B. Make `.capabilities(...)` turn on the family-gated behavior.** Rejected.
  Capabilities do not carry a family, so the translation cannot pick a schema
  ruleset or a forced-choice rule from them. It also changes the meaning of an
  existing method.
- **C. A model-ID-to-family map on the builder or a global registry.** Rejected.
  It is more surface for the same result, and a global registry is hidden
  state.

## Tests

- Acceptance: an application inference profile ARN built with
  `.family(ModelFamily::Anthropic)`, and a `ResponseFormat::JsonSchema`
  request, gives a wire request with the synthesized structured-output tool
  and a forced `toolChoice` (`{ tool: { name } }`).
- Acceptance: the same ARN without the override gives no synthesized tool and
  no `toolChoice` (unchanged behavior).
- The override reaches the capabilities (`structured_output` is `true` for the
  ARN with `.family(Anthropic)`) and the policy (`policy.family()` is
  `Anthropic`).
- `.capabilities(...)` still wins over the override defaults.
- `.family(ModelFamily::Unknown)` on a detectable Anthropic ID turns synthesis
  off.
- A Sonnet 5.5 ID with `.family(ModelFamily::Mistral)` gives the forced-tool
  path (rule A off), and without the override it still gives the native path.

## Left to the builder

- The exact test placement (`builder.rs` tests and `translate/mod.rs` tests
  both have offline helpers; `offline_config` can gain an override variant).
- The exact README and mdBook wording, in Simplified Technical English.

  rejects it once, and rule B moves the handle to native output (this works
  because the policy carries the override family). The cost is one rejected
  request per handle. Document this.

  A would select the native path for a non-Anthropic family. To keep the
  family consistent, `ForcedChoicePolicy::new` sets the static rule only when
  the effective family is `Anthropic`:
  `rejects_static = family == ModelFamily::Anthropic && rejects_forced_tool_choice(model_id)`.

  `rejects_forced_tool_choice` is already `false` for a non-Anthropic detected
  family.

  The ticket names this design. It is one field and one resolved value.
- **B. Make `.capabilities(...)` turn on the family-gated behavior.** Rejected.
  Capabilities do not carry a family, so the translation cannot pick a schema
  ruleset or a forced-choice rule from them. It also changes the meaning of an
  existing method.
- **C. A model-ID-to-family map on the builder or a global registry.** Rejected.
  It is more surface for the same result, and a global registry is hidden
  state.

- Acceptance: an application inference profile ARN built with
  `.family(ModelFamily::Anthropic)`, and a `ResponseFormat::JsonSchema`
  request, gives a wire request with the synthesized structured-output tool
  and a forced `toolChoice` (`{ tool: { name } }`).

  no `toolChoice` (unchanged behavior).
- The override reaches the capabilities (`structured_output` is `true` for the
  ARN with `.family(Anthropic)`) and the policy (`policy.family()` is
  `Anthropic`).
- `.capabilities(...)` still wins over the override defaults.
- `.family(ModelFamily::Unknown)` on a detectable Anthropic ID turns synthesis
  off.
- A Sonnet 5.5 ID with `.family(ModelFamily::Mistral)` gives the forced-tool
  path (rule A off), and without the override it still gives the native path.

- The exact test placement (`builder.rs` tests and `translate/mod.rs` tests
  both have offline helpers; `offline_config` can gain an override variant).
- The exact README and mdBook wording, in Simplified Technical English.

content.text:
## Gate 1: spec approval

**Spec:** `/Users/smaschek/dev/paigasus/paigasus-helikon/.claude/worktrees/sma-837/docs/superpowers/specs/2026-11-21-sma-837-bedrock-family-override-design.md`

**Design in short:** a new method `BedrockModelBuilder::family(ModelFamily)` sets the family directly. `build()` then uses that family and does not detect one from the ID. The resolved family goes to all three places that use it: the request translation (`Config.family`), the default capabilities, and `ForcedChoicePolicy`, which the rule-B fallback reads. `.capabilities(...)` still takes precedence. Without the override, the behavior does not change.

**Challenger verdict:** APPROVE WITH CHANGES. It found no blockers and confirmed that the list of places that use the family is complete.

**Changes I made to the spec:**
- **Tests:** every test now builds the model through the real `build()`. Each test checks that the translation, the policy and the capabilities all see the same family. More tests: a Sonnet 5.5 ID with an override, `ToolChoice::Required`, and rule B running on a model made by the builder.
- **Costs documented:** take a profile ARN that points at Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5. With the override, the first request uses a forced tool choice, and Bedrock rejects it once. Then the model switches to native output. Until it switches, some requests fail locally. Several requests sent at the same time can each get the rejection. A handle built again for each run pays the cost again. The docs will tell users to build one handle and clone it.
- **Rule A gate changed:** the static Sonnet 5.5 / Opus 5.5 rule now applies only when the family supports a forced tool choice. With my first gate, `.family(Unknown)` on a Sonnet 5.5 ID still sent `outputConfig`. With that gate, `.family(Mistral)` also failed every time, with no recovery.
- **Warning:** the builder logs `warn!` when the override is different from a family that the ID clearly names.
- **Docs:** I added a list of existing text to correct, because it tells users to use `.capabilities()`. The examples use `converse(...).sdk_config(...).family(...)`, because `from_env` cannot take the override. The docs also say that the override changes how the tool choice is handled and can cause new local errors.
- **Live check:** I added an `#[ignore]` live test that needs `BEDROCK_PROFILE_ARN`. Nobody has checked that Bedrock returns the same rejection text for a profile ARN. Rule B depends on that text.

**Rejected or postponed:** a `FromStr` for `ModelFamily`, a `BedrockModel::family()` accessor, and an opt-in to native output from the first request. I listed all three as non-goals and possible follow-ups.

**Questions for you:**
1. Does the dev AWS account have an application inference profile on Sonnet 5.5 or Opus 5.5 (or on another Claude model)? If it has one, I run the live test before the merge. If not, the docs say that the profile recovery path is not verified live.
2. Do you want a Linear follow-up ticket for the opt-in to native output from the first request? An example is a builder input that takes the model ID behind the profile.

Do you approve the spec, want changes, or want the challenge run again?

# Writing Plans

## Overview

Write implementation plans for an engineer who has not seen this codebase or this spec. Assume they write idiomatic code in the project's language once they know the exact interface and the exact test, and that they will make a reasonable choice wherever the plan leaves one open. What they cannot know is what you decided: which files, which names and signatures, which values from the spec, which tests prove each task. Document those. Give them the whole plan as bite-sized tasks. DRY. YAGNI. TDD. Frequent commits.

**Announce at start:** "I'm using the writing-plans skill to create the implementation plan."

**Context:** If working in an isolated worktree, it should have been created via the `superpowers:using-git-worktrees` skill at execution time.

**Save plans to:** `docs/superpowers/plans/YYYY-MM-DD-<feature-name>.md`
- (User preferences for plan location override this default)

## Scope Check

If the spec covers multiple independent subsystems, it should have been broken into sub-project specs during brainstorming. If it wasn't, suggest breaking this into separate plans — one per subsystem. Each plan should produce working, testable software on its own.

## File Structure

Before defining tasks, map out which files will be created or modified and what each one is responsible for. This is where decomposition decisions get locked in.

- Design units with clear boundaries and well-defined interfaces. Each file should have one clear responsibility.
- You reason best about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. Prefer smaller, focused files over large ones that do too much.
- Files that change together should live together. Split by responsibility, not by technical layer.
- In existing codebases, follow established patterns. If the codebase uses large files, don't unilaterally restructure - but if a file you're modifying has grown unwieldy, including a split in the plan is reasonable.

This structure informs the task decomposition. Each task should produce self-contained changes that make sense independently.

## Task Right-Sizing

A task is the smallest unit that carries its own test cycle and is worth a
fresh reviewer's gate. When drawing task boundaries: fold setup,
configuration, scaffolding, and documentation steps into the task whose
deliverable needs them; split only where a reviewer could meaningfully
reject one task while approving its neighbor. Each task ends with an
independently testable deliverable.

## Step Granularity

**Each step is one action with a checkable result:**
- "Write the failing test" - step
- "Run it to make sure it fails" - step
- "Implement the minimal code to make the test pass" - step
- "Run the tests and make sure they pass" - step
- "Commit" - step

## Plan Document Header

**Every plan MUST start with this header:**

```markdown
# [Feature Name] Implementation Plan

> **For agentic workers:** REQUIRED SUB-SKILL: Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development (recommended) or superpowers:executing-plans to implement this plan task-by-task. Steps use checkbox (`- [ ]`) syntax for tracking.

**Goal:** [One sentence describing what this builds]

**Architecture:** [2-3 sentences about approach]

**Tech Stack:** [Key technologies/libraries]

**Spec:** [path to the spec/design doc this plan implements — the plan
argues from the spec, so the spec travels with it; executors read both]

## Global Constraints

[The spec's project-wide requirements — version floors, dependency limits,
naming and copy rules, platform requirements — one line each, with exact
values copied verbatim from the spec. Every task's requirements implicitly
include this section.]

## Review Focus

[The five input classes or failure modes the spec implies but no task's
tests exercise that are most likely to bite a person using this software
— one line each, naming the input or condition and the behavior a
reasonable person would expect, most likely first. The spec is a vision
document: it says what the software must do, not everything it will
meet, and its silence on an input is not permission for that input to
break the program. Write the list here, once, with the spec in front of
you. Then, for each line, add the test that pins it to the task that
owns the code, in that task's own step style.]

---
```

## Task Structure

````markdown
### Task N: [Component Name]

**Files:**
- Create: `exact/path/to/file.py`
- Modify: `exact/path/to/existing.py:123-145`
- Test: `tests/exact/path/to/test.py`

**Interfaces:**
- Consumes: [what this task uses from earlier tasks — exact signatures]
- Produces: [what later tasks rely on — exact function names, parameter
  and return types. A task's implementer sees only their own task; this
  block is how they learn the names and types neighboring tasks use.]

- [ ] **Step 1: Write the failing test**

```python
def test_specific_behavior():
    result = function(input)
    assert result == expected
```

- [ ] **Step 2: Run test to verify it fails**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: FAIL with "function not defined"

- [ ] **Step 3: Implement `function(input: InputType) -> ResultType` in `exact/path/to/file.py`**

One line on the approach when the signature and the test leave a choice
(which library call, which data structure); a code block only for an
algorithm they do not determine.

- [ ] **Step 4: Run test to verify it passes**

Run: `pytest tests/path/test.py::test_name -v`
Expected: PASS

- [ ] **Step 5: Commit**

```bash
git add tests/path/test.py src/path/file.py
git commit -m "feat: add specific feature"
```
````

## What a Step Contains

A step is done when the implementer can write exactly one reasonable thing
from it. That is the whole requirement: unambiguous, not complete. Each kind
of step carries what makes it unambiguous and nothing more:

- **A test step:** the test's name and its assertions, as code, with the
  spec's exact values in them.
- **A code step:** the exact signature (name, parameters, return type), the
  file it lives in, and the specific values the spec pins. The implementer
  writes the body. A body appears only for an algorithm the signature and
  tests do not determine, or for exact copy the spec fixes.
- **A verification step:** the command to run and the output that means it
  passed.
- **A reference to another task:** that task's Interfaces block says what
  to use; the plan does not repeat that task's code.

A plan is the set of decisions the implementer cannot make alone. A plan
longer than the code it describes has written the code instead. Lines that
decide nothing ("TBD", "handle edge cases", "add appropriate validation",
"write tests for the above", a type or function no task defines) are the
opposite failure, and the self-review catches both.

## Self-Review

After writing the complete plan, look at the spec with fresh eyes and check the plan against it. This is a checklist you run yourself — not a subagent dispatch.

**1. Spec coverage:** Skim each section/requirement in the spec. Can you point to a task that implements it? List any gaps.

**2. Step scan:** Every step must let the implementer write exactly one reasonable thing, and no step may carry more than that: a line that decides nothing is a gap, a function body the signature and tests already determine is a transcript. Fix both.

**3. Type consistency:** Do the types, method signatures, and property names you used in later tasks match what you defined in earlier tasks? A function called `clearLayers()` in Task 3 but `clearFullLayers()` in Task 7 is a bug.

**4. Review Focus:** For each input class or failure mode the spec implies, is there a task whose tests exercise it? The five uncovered ones most likely to bite a person go in the Review Focus section, and each line there gets its test added to the owning task. An empty section means you checked and found none, not that you skipped the check.

**5. Proportion:** Compare the plan's length to the spec's. A plan several times longer than the spec it implements is a transcript of the program, not a plan. If code blocks are most of the document, replace bodies with signatures, test names and assertions, and check that each step is still unambiguous.

If you find issues, fix them inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on. If you find a spec requirement with no task, add the task.

## Execution Handoff

After saving and self-reviewing the plan, link it for your human partner
to read. If they have already explicitly supplied an execution method, ask
them to review the plan and confirm it captures what they want; wait for that
review before implementation, then use the preserved method. Otherwise, ask
them to review the plan and choose an execution method before implementation.

**When no execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Which execution approach would you prefer?**

- **Subagent-driven** - A fresh subagent implements each task and a fresh reviewer checks it before the next one starts, then a whole-branch review at the end. Most thorough; costs a fresh context per task and per review.
- **Native** - I implement every task myself in this session, the way this harness runs work, then one fresh reviewer on the most capable model checks the whole branch. Cheapest and fastest; no independent review until the end. Runs well with a mid-tier session model, since the plan carries the design.

**For this plan I recommend <one of the two>, because <one sentence from the plan: how much the tasks depend on each other's interfaces, how many there are, what a shipped mistake would cost>. Does the plan capture what you want, and which approach should we use?"**

**When an execution method has already been supplied:**

**"Plan complete and saved to `docs/superpowers/plans/<filename>.md`. Please review the plan. Does it capture what you want?"**

**If Subagent-driven chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:subagent-driven-development

**If Native chosen:**
- **REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use superpowers:executing-plans
